fields.text: Make a two-frame story through a handoff between models. Muse establishes the opening. Nano Banana stages the next beat from that actual image. Gemini compares both frames; Muse Edit uses the draft, original reference and those concrete notes for one fixed revision. A fresh Gemini pass inspects the repaired pixels. Five paid calls, including two independent visual readings; this is one revision, not a conditional retry loop. Save the opening, draft, repaired frame and final notes. A remaining flaw never discards the artwork. Image catalog subtotal $0.059 on 12 September 2026, plus two vision/text calls.

First frame of an original two-scene story. A small red crab kite-maker stands on a sun-bleached wooden jetty over a shallow turquoise salt lagoon. It has two large claws, four small walking legs visible, round black eyes, and a floppy straw hat with a violet ribbon. One claw holds a wound white string reel; beside it rests a single yellow diamond kite with exactly two violet tail bows. The crab looks toward a flat pink sandbar across the water. Bold cut-paper collage, crisp torn-paper edges, coral-red, yellow, turquoise and pale pink, bright overhead sun. Wide 3:2 composition; entire crab, reel, kite and jetty visible. No robots, space stations, glass capsules, plants, text, panel borders or watermark.

Create the next story beat on the pink sandbar across the lagoon. The same crab braces its legs and leans backward as the yellow diamond kite lifts overhead in a strong breeze. The white string visibly connects the kite to the reel in one claw; the other claw keeps the straw hat from blowing away. Exactly two violet bows remain on the kite's tail. Show the kite fully in frame and make the new wind-driven action clear. Retain the crisp cut-paper collage and sunlit coral/yellow/turquoise/pink palette. This is a new story action, not the original jetty picture with a changed background. No extra crabs or kites, lettering or panel borders.

Preserve the red crab's body shape, black eyes, two claws, straw hat and violet ribbon. Keep one yellow diamond kite, two violet tail bows, and the white reel/string. The string should connect reel and kite in frame 2; the kite must be flying rather than resting. The scene moves from a wooden jetty to a pink sandbar. Preserve cut-paper materials, crisp edges and bright sunlit palette; do not inherit any robot, greenhouse or space-scene details.

fields.sep:
The text above describes the first scene; the supplied reference image is its actual rendered result. Make ONE new full-frame image that continues that scene. Preserve the reference character and visual style while showing the different action below. Treat the next beat as a change of story state, not a request to repeat the opening composition.

NEXT BEAT:

nodes.name: Nano Banana stages the next beat

fields.system: You are a film continuity reader comparing TWO actual images. Image 1 is the opening frame; image 2 is the draft next frame. The text contains the opening brief, next beat, and continuity requirements. Inspect the pixels of both images; requested details are not proof they appeared. In at most 200 words: state the visible story action in each frame; list up to four concrete identity, prop-count, state or composition mismatches, with observations from both frames; then give the smallest specific correction needed while retaining the new action. Prioritize duplicated story-critical objects and impossible handoffs over cosmetic changes. Distinguish intended story changes from errors. Mark an obscured or small detail unclear instead of inventing it. If no meaningful mismatch is visible, say so and request preservation of the draft. Do not invent measurements, scores, confidence percentages, universal PASS/FAIL, or publish-readiness guarantees. These advisory notes will guide exactly one revision.

fields.sep:
REVISE THE ATTACHED DRAFT ONCE. Image 1 is the DRAFT NEXT FRAME to correct; image 2 is the ORIGINAL OPENING FRAME used only as an identity and style anchor. Preserve image 1's intended new action and story state. Keep its staging unless a specific continuity requirement makes a change necessary. Use the story and continuity requirements above plus the observed draft notes below. Fix only supported mismatches; do not invent a new scene, duplicate subjects or props, merge frames, add labels, or copy the opening action. If the notes report no meaningful mismatch, preserve the draft with minimal change. Produce one complete next-frame image, not a collage or before/after comparison.

ACTUAL DRAFT CONTINUITY NOTES:

fields.system: Independently compare TWO actual images. Image 1 is the original opening; image 2 is the repaired next frame. You have the original story brief, next beat and continuity requirements, not the earlier review. Inspect the repaired pixels yourself; never assume a repair worked. In at most 300 words write: (1) Story beat: what visibly happens in each frame and whether the new action reads clearly. (2) A compact table of three to six important continuity features with observations from each image and status consistent, changed, or unclear. Distinguish intended story changes from accidental identity, prop-count, state, style or composition drift. Prioritize duplicated story-critical objects and impossible handoffs. (3) Director's note: the most useful remaining correction, or one specific strength if none is evident. If a small or obscured detail cannot be judged, say so. Do not invent measurements, numerical scores, confidence percentages, automatic PASS/FAIL, or a guarantee of publish-readiness. These are final advisory notes about the images you actually see; the run performs no further repair.
